transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Crownwood - Head of ML), Ravi Kapoor (CTO), Lena Ortiz (VP Finance)

Summary (auto-gen, may be rough): Quick cost economics discovery for hosted vs dedicated vs private. Customer wants to understand per-1k token economics, how batching and KV/prefix caching reduce effective token volume, and what Reserved/Dedicated discount tiers look like for commit levels. They also want security docs and a short pilot.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for carving out time, I'm Jordan from Redwood, with Samir our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Maya: Hi, good, thanks. Sorry ran over a previous meeting so jumping in a bit late but yeah excited to dig in.
[00:12] Ravi: Morning all, quick intros on our side I'm ravi cto, maya leads the ml effort and lena is finance so she'll cover budgets.
[00:18] Lena: Hi all.
[00:22] Jordan: Cool. Today we wanted to focus on the unit economics piece you called out; get a sense for your token volumes, latency SLOs, and what budgets look like so we can recommend hosted vs dedicated or a private deployment. Maya, do you want to kick off with your expected workload?
[00:34] Maya: Sure, high level — we're launching a recommendation assistant for our advisors. Peak qps around 120 requests per second, average prompt size is about 1.2k tokens incl. context, expected steady state about 200-300M tokens per month initially, could grow to 1B in 12 months if the pilot goes well. Latency target is 200-300ms p50 for the user flows, p95 we want under 800ms.
[00:58] Samir: Got it. That's helpful. Just to ground the pricing conversation — do you have a current per-1k token benchmark or target? Many teams look at $/1k tokens as a baseline.
[01:08] Maya: We're trying to stay under $10k a month for the pilot phase, ideally closer to 6-8k. But that's total infra + API cost, so want to understand what Redwood would look like.
[01:18] Jordan: Right. For a dataset like that — 200-300M tokens — we've seen two common approaches. Hosted is fastest to get started: no infra, straightforward pricing. Dedicated/reserved will typically give you 30-50% lower per-1k token than hosted at mid to high commits, and private/VPC has a similar delta but with added ops overhead. Also, cache and batching drastically change effective token counts.
[01:38] Ravi: Can you give us concrete numbers? Even ballpark ranges would help.
[01:42] Jordan: Sure. For examples we often show: hosted for our curated Llama-family variants might land in the range of $0.03 to $0.08 per 1k tokens depending on model size and call patterns. For dedicated with a 12-month commit we typically hit roughly 30-40% discount off hosted list for that same model family. So that moves you to maybe $0.02 to $0.05 per 1k tokens.
[02:05] Lena: So at 200M tokens a month at $0.05 per 1k tokens, what is that math?
[02:10] Samir: Quick calc — 200M tokens is 200,000 units of 1k tokens. At $0.05/1k that's $10,000 a month. If you negotiate to $0.03/1k that's $6,000. If caching reduces your effective token volume by 30% you'd be paying on 140M tokens, so about $4.2k at $0.03/1k.
[02:27] Maya: That actually maps pretty well to the finance target for the pilot (6-8k). Good to see how caching kicks it down. Can you explain the caching and batching levers more specifically?
[02:36] Samir: Yeah. There are two big levers: prefix/KV caching and batching. Prefix/KV cache means we store earlier tokens or model KV states for repeated context — for example, system prompts, user profiles, static context — and we don't re-send those as tokens to the model. For recommendation flows we often get 20-40% cache hit rates out of the box depending on how much shared context you have.
[02:56] Samir: Batching is about combining multiple user requests into a single GPU forward pass. For models with short to medium prompts and when latency SLO allows a few tens of ms extra, batching can reduce per-token compute cost by 15-35% depending on distribution. On Dedicated you also get better packing and lower tail latency to keep p95 reasonable.
[03:17] Ravi: So are those caching and batching savings additive? Like can we expect 50% total savings?
[03:21] Samir: They can be roughly additive but there's overlap. A conservative expectation is 30% combined savings; aggressive tuning for your workload might hit 50% if you have high cacheability and can tolerate batching windows. We can run a small benchmark with your prompt set to measure this.
[03:35] Maya: What's the difference in model quality between the cheaper variants and the more expensive ones? We can't degrade accuracy too much.
[03:40] Samir: Good question. We surface a model catalog with verified perf profiles — for many tasks the quantized 4-bit variants or smaller open models are within a few percentage points of the larger model on recommendation accuracy. If your eval set is sensitive we recommend we run side-by-side evals on your prompts; sometimes hybrid routing is best — send critical flows to the high-quality variant and lower tier to cheaper variants. That also helps unit economics.
[04:02] Jordan: Also worth noting burst capacity: on Dedicated you reserve baseline capacity and can buy burst on-demand. If you're peaky, that affects commit sizing and pricing. Our pricing sheet shows a baseline price and then an overage or burst price. For pilots we often recommend a small dedicated pool for predictable throughput plus a hosted fallback.
[04:18] Lena: From a procurement angle — what are the commercial terms? Minimum commitment lengths, payment terms?
[04:22] Jordan: Typical reserved contracts are 6 or 12 months with better pricing for 12-months. Payment net-30 is common; enterprise PA/POs we can sign. We'll share the procurement checklist and our standard MSA and SOW. For pilots we can often do a month-to-month evaluation with a credit or a short pilot agreement.
[04:38] Lena: Great. Security — we need SOC2 type II, SSO, KMS integration and we have some data residency constraints for EU customers. How does Redwood support that?
[04:46] Samir: We support SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS integration and for Private/VPC options we can deploy into your VPC or provide a customer-managed network. We have SOC2 docs and ISO paperwork — Jordan will send over the package. For EU data residency we can route requests to a region in eu-west-1 or set up private deployment depending on compliance needs.
[05:06] Maya: For the benchmark, what telemetry/metrics do you need from our side?
[05:10] Samir: Ideally a representative prompt set with labels, expected QPS pattern (time-of-day), and an evaluation metric file so we can run accuracy and latency tradeoffs. Also an example of statefulness — e.g., whether you need long context or user-specific KV that affects cache hit rate.
[05:21] Ravi: On the dedicated sizing — what GPU types are typical? What's the difference in per-token compute cost between say an A100 vs H100 or newer chips?
[05:30] Samir: Our platform supports a range. H100 gives higher throughput on larger models and can reduce latency at similar batch sizes; cost per GPU hour is higher, so the per-token compute cost depends on utilization and model. For many open models an A100-80GB or equivalent is cost-effective. We'll include a short performance map in the benchmark packet.
[05:46] Maya: One practical question: how do you measure 'effective token' after caching? Is that billing or internal?
[05:51] Jordan: Billing is on the tokens sent to the model. We provide both raw token counts and an 'effective token' metric after cache hits; for dedicated with application-level caching we can provide aggregated reports so you see savings. Our console shows token-level cost breakdown per route and per model.
[06:05] Lena: In terms of discounts, is there an up-front credit or committed spend rebate?
[06:09] Jordan: For larger commits we do a committed monthly spend with reduced per-1k pricing; there can also be upfront credits baked into the contract depending on term-length and size. We'll propose two example commit tiers in the pricing sheet — small pilot commit and mid-tier commit with deeper discounts.
[06:22] Maya: That sounds right. Would you recommend we start on hosted or go straight to a small dedicated pool?
[06:27] Samir: For your numbers and latency SLO p95 under 800ms, we recommend a small dedicated pool plus hosted fallback. Dedicated helps with predictable tail latency and gives much better unit economics once you hit steady traffic. For the pilot we can size a 2-4 GPU pool that covers your baseline and run load tests to refine.
[06:42] Ravi: If we did a 3-GPU dedicated pool for baseline and then rely on hosted for bursts, how does pricing blend? Is there a blended rate?
[06:48] Jordan: We'll show blended examples in the sheet. The blended cost equals committed cost + on-demand for burst computed across expected burst volume. It's straightforward math once we have your qps profile.
[06:56] Maya: Any gotchas around rate limits or request shaping we should design for?
[07:00] Samir: Two things — first, your client should implement exponential backoff for transient errors. Second, route-aware client logic helps (send critical requests to the high-quality model/region). We also expose per-route quotas and per-key rate limits. For batch-friendly flows, adding a short buffer (30-100ms) to allow batching improves efficiency.
[07:15] Lena: How long before we can run a pilot? Assuming we get internal approval this week.
[07:19] Jordan: For a dedicated pilot we can usually stand up a small pool in 3-5 business days if there are no networking constraints. If you need VPC/private deployment it may be 2-3 weeks depending on networking approvals.
[07:29] Maya: About the evaluation: we need to run accuracy comparisons on our holdout set. Will you run the eval on our behalf or provide tooling?
[07:35] Samir: We can run it for you if you provide the prompt set and labels, or we can give you scripts to run locally. For the pilot we typically run both — our bench on our infra and your runbook to validate parity.
[07:46] Ravi: What's the expected OPEX for operating private on-prem? I assume that adds infra cost and ops but maybe lowers unit cost?
[07:52] Samir: Private on-prem gives you more control but you take on hardware and ops; unit compute cost can be lower at scale but the break-even depends on utilization and amortization. We typically recommend private for regulated workloads or when you have sustained, high utilization that justifies infra.
[08:08] Jordan: To summarize the high level we heard: 200-300M tokens/month pilot, latency p50 200-300ms, p95 under 800ms, budget for pilot ~6-10k. Key asks: hosted vs dedicated cost breakdown, benchmarking on your prompt set, security docs and procurement checklist, and a proposal for a small dedicated pilot with burst fallback.
[08:29] Maya: Yep that covers it.
[08:31] Lena: We'll need the pricing sheet and scope doc by early next week to get procurement moving.
[08:35] Jordan: We'll send the pricing sheet and security package by Friday. Samir will upload a benchmark template and we can get a pilot kickoff on the calendar.
[08:42] Maya: One more question, on the caching: how do you handle stale personalization data if we use KV caching?
[08:48] Samir: We expose TTLs and eviction policies; you can use per-user keys and versioning. For personalization we typically do short-lived cache entries (tens of minutes) and add version keys when user state changes. We can also scrub sensitive fields before caching depending on your compliance requirements.
[09:05] Ravi: For billing transparency, can we get a sample console export that shows token breakdown per route/model?
[09:10] Jordan: Yes, we'll include a sample cost export and screenshots of the console.
[09:14] Lena: Okay great. If you could also flag any legal/po requirements we should prep, that helps.
[09:18] Jordan: Will do.
[09:20] Maya: Thanks, this was helpful.
[09:22] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and proposed pilot dates.

(Transcript notes: occasional mis-hears by auto-transcript; filler words like uh/um removed occasionally. There is some overlap on speakers.)

End of meeting.
